summary.text: Cell signaling is the process by which a cell interacts with itself, with other cells, and with the environment, and it is a fundamental property of all forms of life.
A signaling process typically involves a first messenger called a ligand, a receptor, and the signal itself, and the signals are mostly chemical.
Signals can act on the same cell, on nearby cells, or on distant cells, which are called autocrine, paracrine and endocrine signaling.

facts.label: Five signal types
facts.value: Autocrine, intracrine, juxtacrine, paracrine and endocrine

facts.label: Ligand examples
facts.value: Ions, lipids, peptides, carbohydrates and nucleic acids

facts.label: Hormone carrier
facts.value: Endocrine signals are usually carried by the blood

facts.label: Membrane receptor types
facts.value: Ion channel linked, G-protein coupled and enzyme linked

facts.label: Quorum sensing
facts.value: First observed in a marine bacterium that glows when dense

items.prompt: A cell is exposed to a polar, water-loving peptide hormone. Where is the receptor that responds to it?

options.label: Embedded in the cell membrane, since the peptide cannot diffuse across it
Inside the nucleus, since hormones always reach the DNA
Inside the cytoplasm, since peptides diffuse in freely
On the outside of the blood vessel that carried it

items.explain: Peptides are polar and hydrophilic, so they cannot diffuse freely across the plasma membrane and act through a membrane-bound receptor.

items.prompt: A steroid hormone dissolves in fats and reaches a target cell. What happens next?

options.label: It binds a receptor on the outer surface and never enters the cell
It is broken down at the membrane and only its pieces get in
It crosses the membrane and a carrier takes it to the nucleus to switch on genes
It stays outside and switches the cell on from a distance

items.explain: Lipid-soluble ligands diffuse through the plasma membrane, bind cytoplasmic transporters that carry them into the nucleus, and activate specific genes.

items.prompt: A gland releases a hormone into the bloodstream, and it acts on an organ far away. What kind of signaling is this?

options.label: Autocrine signaling
Endocrine signaling
Paracrine signaling
Juxtacrine signaling

items.explain: Endocrine signaling occurs between distant cells, with the signal (hormone) usually carried by the blood.

items.prompt: A handful of receptors on a cell are activated, yet the cell responds strongly. What can explain this?

options.label: Each receptor releases a hormone into the blood
The ligand copies itself many times over
Each receptor splits into many receptors
A second messenger system that amplifies the original signal

items.explain: Second messenger systems can amplify a signal: activation of a few receptors results in multiple secondary messengers being activated.

items.prompt: A cell responds to a change in pressure on its surface. Which class of receptor most likely senses it?

options.label: Ion channel linked receptors, with a ligand-activated gate
G-protein coupled receptors, which open a gate
Intracellular receptors, which bind steroid hormones
Enzyme linked receptors, which make second messengers

items.explain: Most receptors activated by physical stimuli such as pressure or temperature are ion channel receptors.

items.prompt: A marine bacterium glows only when many of its neighbours are around. What process lets single cells respond to the crowd?

options.label: Endocrine signaling, where blood carries the glow signal
Quorum sensing, where cells make and detect a signaling molecule
Steroid signaling, where a hormone enters the nucleus
Juxtacrine signaling, where two cells touch

items.explain: Quorum sensing lets individuals begin an activity only when the population is large, through production and detection of a signaling molecule.
